anchors.title: Texas grid reliability: Are we ready for the next storm?
anchors.body:
It's been nearly five years since Winter Storm Uri exposed catastrophic failures in the Texas power grid. ERCOT remains isolated from the national grid, and while some weatherization requirements have been implemented, many experts question whether they're sufficient.

Are we actually better prepared now than we were in 2021? What would another major winter storm mean for Texas families?

comments.body: I lost power for 4 days during Uri. Pipes burst, $15,000 in damage to my home. My elderly neighbor had to be hospitalized. This isn't an abstract policy debate for those of us who lived through it.

replies.body: My electricity bill that month was over $3,000 because I was on a variable-rate plan. A lot of people didn't even know they were on those plans until the crisis hit.

comments.body: Connecting to the national grid means accepting federal regulation. That's the real reason Texas keeps ERCOT independent — it's about deregulation, not reliability.

replies.body: Energy independence means nothing when the power is off and people are dying. At some point, sovereignty becomes a talking point that costs lives.

anchors.title: Proposal: Require weather-hardening for all Texas power plants
anchors.body:
I propose that the Texas Legislature mandate comprehensive winterization standards for all power generation facilities operating within ERCOT, with compliance verified by independent inspectors. This would include insulation of critical components, backup fuel supplies, and cold-weather operational testing.

The cost would be funded through a small surcharge on electricity bills — estimated at $3-5 per month for the average household. This is a fraction of what Texans paid during Uri.
